title: Will AI Replace Social Workers? What Students in Policy, Nonprofit and Social Impact Work Need to Know
summary: Will AI replace social workers? What 2026 data says on social work, policy, grant writing and nonprofit jobs, which roles shrink, and how to get started.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


• Will AI replace social workers? No. BLS projects social workers to grow 6% from 2025 to 2035, and mental health and substance abuse social workers 10.3%. AI is taking documentation and first drafts, not the relationship with a client.


• Policy research is the most exposed work in this field: Microsoft ranks political scientists 9th of 785 occupations for AI applicability.


• The tight 2025-26 entry market in government and nonprofits comes mostly from hiring freezes and funding cuts, not from AI.


• Your move: pair a people skill with a data or writing skill, learn the rules for using AI with client data, and get real project experience.


[Externships](https://www.extern.com/post/what-is-an-externship) are short, remote professional experience programs where you work on real projects for real companies, with guidance from people in the field. The[Khan Academy Strategic Partnerships & Growth Externship](https://www.extern.com/externships/khan-academy-strategic-partnerships-earned-revenue-nov-2026) and the[ARCeH Data Analytics, Health Outcomes Externship](https://www.extern.com/externships/arceh-childrens-environmental-health-analytics-nov-2026) give you mission-driven project work to point to.[Explore all Externships](https://www.extern.com/externships) .


---


## Will AI Replace Social Workers and Other Social Impact Jobs?


No. Social work, nonprofit management and fundraising are all projected to grow through 2035, and the most human parts of them are the least exposed to AI. What AI changes is the paperwork around the work. The verdict for this field is "transforming," and the bigger threat to your first job right now is funding, not software.


### The Short Answer


**AI won't replace social workers, but it's already rewriting their paperwork.** The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects[social workers](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/community-and-social-service/social-workers.htm) to grow 6% between 2025 and 2035, with about 69,100 openings a year. Mental health and substance abuse social workers grow fastest, at 10.3%, and BLS rates them only "Moderate" for AI exposure. That's the lowest rating of any role in this article.


But policy work is a different story. Research, summaries and memo drafts are exactly what AI tools do well, so junior policy research is changing fast.


In our one-on-one sessions with students headed into social impact work, the fear we hear most is "Will there be anything left for me to do?" Fair question. But when we dig into the data, the honest answer is that AI is the smaller of two problems. The larger one is money. For the broad view across every field, see our guide to[jobs AI won't replace](https://www.extern.com/post/jobs-ai-wont-replace-guide) .


### The AI Exposure Scorecard for Policy, Nonprofit and Social Impact Roles


Same five rows as every article in this series. Exposure is high on the research side and lower on the people side.


Scorecard row Policy, nonprofit and social impact roles (as of November 2026)


**Task exposure** BLS AI exposure (August 2026): social workers High, mental health and substance abuse social workers Moderate, fundraisers High; political scientists, community service managers and planners Very high. Microsoft ranks political scientists 9th of 785 occupations, fundraisers 456th.


**Job outlook** BLS 2025-35: social workers +6%, mental health social workers +10.3%, community service managers +7.2%, fundraisers +5.5%, political scientists -2.0%. Average: +3.5%.


**Entry-level hiring signal** Weak, mainly for funding reasons: federal hiring fell in 2025 (Brookings). Extern's tracker: 116 policy internship listings from 69 employers (August to November 2026).


**Most exposed role** Junior policy research analyst; eligibility interviewer


**Least exposed role** Mental health and clinical social worker; fundraiser


**Verdict** Transforming (the squeeze is funding cuts, not AI)


One caution on exposure. BLS says its[AI exposure categories](https://www.bls.gov/emp/publications/ai-exposure-categories.htm) don't imply job loss. Microsoft's[applicability scores](https://github.com/microsoft/working-with-ai) measure where Copilot use overlaps a job's tasks, which isn't a forecast either.


## What Parts of Social Work and Policy Work Is AI Already Doing?


AI already drafts case notes, emails, grant proposals and research summaries, and governments use it for record summaries and call-center bots. In nearly every case a person reviews the output, and the decisions that affect a family, a grantee or a policy stay with people.


### Case Notes and Documentation


Social work runs on documentation, and that's where AI landed first. **A[2026 NASW and UT Austin survey](https://www.socialworkers.org/News/News-Releases/ID/3437/National-Survey-Finds-Most-Social-Workers-Already-Using-Artificial-Intelligence-Calling-For-Ethical-Guidance-and-Professional-Leadership) of 1,179 social workers found most already use AI** , mainly for emails, reports, documentation and research. Two-thirds said their most pressing need is clear ethical guidelines.


Task What AI does today What still needs a person


**Case notes** Transcribes and drafts notes after a visit The social worker edits, checks and files them


**Emails and reports** Drafts routine correspondence and summaries Tone, accuracy and confidentiality calls


**Risk screening** Some agencies score hotline calls Screeners decide and can override the score


**Grant proposals** Drafts applications, reports and donor emails Funder relationships, strategy and checking every claim


**Policy research** Summarizes studies and drafts memos Judgment, stakeholder access and political reading


**Public benefits intake** Call-center bots and record summaries Eligibility decisions and hard cases


Risk screening is the controversial one, and it's a reminder that "AI can do it" and "AI should decide it" are different questions.


### Grant Writing and Fundraising


Drafting is everywhere. Autonomous fundraising isn't:


• **Drafting is common.** In the Center for Effective Philanthropy's[2025 "AI With Purpose" report](https://cep.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/CEP_AI_Layout_FINAL.pdf) , 61% of nonprofits using AI applied it to fundraising, including drafting grant applications and reports.


• **Advanced tools are rare.** Nonprofit Tech for Good found in[January 2026](https://www.nptechforgood.com/2026/01/09/new-data-reveals-most-nonprofits-arent-using-ai-for-fundraising/) that only 2.3% of 826 nonprofits use predictive major-donor AI.


• **Funders aren't automating their side.** In Candid's[2025 foundation survey](https://candid.org/blogs/will-foundations-soon-use-ai-to-screen-grant-applications/) , 1% of foundations used AI to screen applicants and 97% didn't.


So the first draft of a grant is now cheap. The relationship with the program officer isn't.


### AI in the Public Sector


Governments are mostly piloting. Federal agencies reported 3,611 AI use cases in 2025,[according to Nextgov](https://www.nextgov.com/artificial-intelligence/2026/04/agencies-report-over-3000-ai-use-cases-2025/412898/) , with HHS listing the most (447) and the VA using AI to summarize clinical data and run a call-center VoiceBot. State tech chiefs ranked AI their top priority for 2026, the first time it beat cybersecurity, in[NASCIO's annual survey](https://www.nascio.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/NASCIO-2026-State-Top-10-Priorities_a11y.pdf) .


But piloting isn't the same as replacing staff.[Code for America's May 2026 assessment](https://codeforamerica.org/news/code-for-america-unveils-second-annual-government-ai-landscape-assessment/) found nearly every state has run AI pilots, while very few have built AI into core operations. Nonprofits abroad use it too: CEP's report describes Mercy Corps comparing a decade of satellite crop data with real-time data to find the most vulnerable areas in Sudan. People still decided where the aid went.


## What Does the Job Data Actually Say?


The data says social impact jobs are still growing, the tiny policy research field is shrinking slightly, and the tough 2025-26 market for new grads has more to do with federal hiring and funding than with AI. Early-career AI research exists, but it doesn't cover this sector well.


### BLS: Social Impact Jobs Keep Growing


**According to the[BLS 2025-35 projections](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/ecopro_08272026.htm) , community and social service occupations will grow 7.4%, about twice the 3.5% average.** Social and community service managers, the job title for many nonprofit program directors, grow 7.2%. Fundraisers grow 5.5%.


The one shrinking number is easy to misread. Political scientists are projected to fall 2.0%, but that's a field of about 6,100 jobs with 400 openings a year. Most people doing policy analysis aren't classified as political scientists at all. So it's a signal about research-heavy roles, not about every policy job.


### The Real Squeeze Is Funding, Not AI


And here's what makes this field different from most in this series. When new grads tell us government and nonprofit hiring feels frozen, they're right, and AI isn't the main reason. So what is?


[Brookings reported in April 2026](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/assessing-the-state-of-ai-adoption-across-the-federal-government/) that federal AI job postings fell along with the broader drop in federal hiring in 2025, and only 160 full-time federal listings explicitly required AI expertise that year. Those are budget decisions. Blaming AI for them would point you at the wrong problem.


### From Extern's Data


We track US internship postings daily. Policy internships turn out to be spread across very different employers:


• **116 listings from 69 employers.** That's how many policy internship postings Extern's tracker logged from August to November 2026.


• **Who posts the most.**[Disney](https://www.extern.com/post/disney-internship-guide) (8), the International Rescue Committee (7), Brave Health (5),[Xcel Energy](https://www.extern.com/post/xcel-energy-internship-guide) (5) and[Sanofi](https://www.extern.com/post/sanofi-internship-guide) (5). They aren't Extern partners, just the top posters in our data.


• **Not just think tanks.** A media company, a humanitarian NGO, a health company and a utility all hire policy interns. Our[International Rescue Committee internship guide](https://www.extern.com/post/international-rescue-committee-internship-guide) covers the NGO route.


But only eight of those postings published pay. Too few for a reliable number, so we're leaving it out.


### The Early-Career Research


Stanford's Digital Economy Lab reported in[August 2026](https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/news/canariesaug26/) that employment for 22- to 25-year-olds in highly AI-exposed jobs is about 19% below the path of less-exposed peers, mostly through fewer hires. The authors don't claim AI caused it. And they flag public administration as a sector where their payroll data and national surveys disagree most, so we wouldn't apply that figure to government work. Honestly, nobody has good AI-specific data on nonprofit hiring yet.


## Which Policy and Nonprofit Jobs Are Safest, and Which Are Most at Risk?


The safest roles rest on relationships, licensure and community trust: clinical social workers, fundraisers and program managers. The most exposed are research-heavy and rules-based roles: junior policy researchers and benefits eligibility interviewers. Most roles sit in between and are projected to grow anyway.


### Seven Roles Compared


Exposure combines the BLS category and Microsoft's ranking; outlook is BLS 2025-35.


Role AI exposure BLS outlook 2025-35 Why


**Mental health or clinical social worker** Low to medium (BLS Moderate; Microsoft rank 383) +10.3% Therapeutic relationship, licensure and crisis judgment; AI touches notes only


**Fundraiser or grant writer** Medium (BLS High; Microsoft rank 456) +5.5% First drafts automate; donor and funder trust don't


**Nonprofit program manager** Medium (BLS Very high; Microsoft rank 360) +7.2% (community service managers) Reporting automates; leading staff, budgets and partnerships doesn't


**Child, family and school social worker** Medium to high (BLS High; Microsoft rank 39) +4.4% Documentation-heavy, but home visits and safety decisions stay human


**Urban and regional planner** Medium to high (BLS Very high; Microsoft rank 48) +3.9% Reports and mapping get AI help; public meetings and approvals don't


**Eligibility interviewer (government programs)** High (BLS Very high; Microsoft rank 114) +1.6% Rules-based intake and verification are automatable


**Policy research analyst (political scientist proxy)** High (BLS Very high; Microsoft rank 9) -2.0%, a small field Research synthesis and memo drafting are core AI strengths

### The Pattern


Writing, research and intake paperwork shrink. Relationships, licensed judgment and community leadership grow.


A rough test: if a task can be done from a desk with a template, AI is coming for part of it. If it needs someone trusted in the room, it isn't. That's a simplification, of course, since a child welfare caseworker does both in the same afternoon.


## How Is AI Changing Entry-Level Work in Policy and Nonprofits?


The junior research and drafting work changes first: AI writes the literature review and the memo's first draft, and the new hire checks it and adds what AI can't know. In social work, entry stays protected by licensure, but documentation now comes with AI rules you're expected to know.


### The Junior Research Job Is Changing First


A first-year research assistant at a think tank or advocacy group used to spend weeks on literature reviews and memo drafts. That's the work AI does best, so expect the job to tilt toward verifying sources, pulling local data and talking to the people a policy affects. That's our inference from the task data, not a survey of employers. We could be wrong about the speed. We don't think we're wrong about the direction.


### Social Work: Documentation Changes, Licensure Doesn't


Clinical social work still needs a master's degree, supervised field hours and a license. None of that's automatable. What's new is the paperwork layer. NASW's[AI and social work guidance page](https://www.socialworkers.org/About/Ethics/AI-and-Social-Work) warns about exposing client data to third-party vendors and tells practitioners to vet tools and strip identifiers.


Yet most employers haven't caught up. A[University at Buffalo study](https://www.buffalo.edu/news/releases/2026/08/Professional-social-work-bodies-providing-little-guidance-for-AI-use.html) of 103 MSW-level social workers (August 2026) found most get little AI guidance at work. So a new grad who already knows the privacy rules is useful from week one.


### Nonprofits Have a Skills Gap You Can Fill


In CEP's 2025 survey, 58% of nonprofit leaders named a lack of staff expertise as a top AI concern. Their other worries were inaccurate output (73%) and data security (67%). Read that from the hiring side: a junior who can use AI carefully, check its claims and protect client data solves a problem leadership already has. Nobody surveyed hiring managers on exactly this, so treat it as our reading.


## What Skills Make You Hard to Replace in Social Impact Work?


The durable skills mix people work with careful use of data and AI: responsible AI and privacy, program evaluation, grant writing with verified claims, policy memo writing, community facilitation and a licensure track. Each is provable with something you've made or done.


### Six Skills and How to Prove Them


1. **Responsible AI and privacy for client data.** Write a one-page AI-use protocol for a student org or volunteer site based on NASW's guidance on de-identification and vendor vetting.


2. **Program evaluation and data analysis.** Excel, R or Tableau, plus logic models. Prove it with an evaluation of a real program using public Census data. Our piece on[whether data analysts will be replaced by AI](https://www.extern.com/post/will-ai-replace-data-analysts-guide) shows where that skill set is heading.


3. **Grant writing with verified claims.** A mock grant with a fact-checked evidence appendix shows you can use AI for drafts without trusting it blindly.


4. **Policy memo writing.** Two or three published briefs or op-eds, or a public comment submitted on regulations.gov.


5. **Community engagement and facilitation.** Leading public meetings, coalition work or a volunteer program. Bilingual skills count double here.


6. **A licensure track (for social work).** BSW or MSW field placement hours are the strongest moat in this whole field.


Having coached students through career pivots for years, we notice the same thing: the ones who get hired in social impact can show one finished thing, not a list of causes they care about.


## How Can You Get AI-Ready Social Impact Experience as a Student?


Apply on the government and nonprofit calendars, build one evaluation or policy project yourself, and get real project experience with a mission-driven organization. The project is what lets you talk about impact with evidence.


### Internship Programs and Timing


If you're reading this in November 2026, here's where summer 2027 stands:


1. **Federal and congressional programs.** Many agencies and think tanks recruit from fall through winter, and some federal roles need months of lead time. Our[government internships guide](https://www.extern.com/post/government-internships-summer-2027-guide) has the month-by-month list.


2. **Think tanks.** Their timelines are often more flexible. Start with our[Brookings Institution internship guide](https://www.extern.com/post/brookings-institution-internship-guide) .


3. **Nonprofits and NGOs.** Large organizations tend to post between fall and January, and smaller ones often wait for spring grant cycles. The[nonprofit and social impact internships guide](https://www.extern.com/post/nonprofit-social-impact-internships-summer-2027-guide) covers both.


### Externships for Social Impact Students


An Externship gives you a finished project with a real organization, remotely, in 4 to 11 weeks (most commonly 8), with an extern manager guiding you. Two November 2026 options fit this field:


• The[Khan Academy Strategic Partnerships & Growth Externship](https://www.extern.com/externships/khan-academy-strategic-partnerships-earned-revenue-nov-2026) , for students drawn to nonprofit partnerships and earned revenue, the business side of mission work.


• The[ARCeH Data Analytics, Health Outcomes Externship](https://www.extern.com/externships/arceh-childrens-environmental-health-analytics-nov-2026) , where you turn public health data into analysis, close to the program evaluation skill above.


94% of students rated their Extern experience positively in our 2026 post-program survey. At Extern, we've seen social impact students get the most out of a project when they treat it like a grant report: what was the problem, what did you do, what changed. ## Frequently Asked Questions


### Will social workers be replaced by AI?


No. BLS projects social workers to grow 6% from 2025 to 2035, with about 69,100 openings a year, and rates mental health and substance abuse social workers only "Moderate" for AI exposure. AI is drafting case notes and emails. Home visits, crisis calls and licensed clinical judgment still need a person.


### How is AI used in social work?


Mostly for paperwork. A 2026 NASW and UT Austin survey of 1,179 social workers found most already use AI for emails, reports and documentation. Some agencies also use risk-screening tools, which is controversial. Social workers still review everything, and two-thirds of respondents want clearer ethical guidelines.


### Will AI replace therapists and counselors?


Not on current evidence. Among social workers, the mental health and substance abuse group is BLS's least AI-exposed and fastest growing, at 10.3% from 2025 to 2035. Therapy depends on trust and licensure. AI may help with notes and scheduling, but the session itself stays human.


### Will AI replace grant writers?


It's replacing first drafts, not grant writers. CEP found 61% of nonprofits using AI apply it to fundraising, including drafting applications. But a 2024 Candid survey found 23% of foundations won't accept AI-generated applications and 67% were undecided. Funders trust people, so relationships and accurate claims matter more.


### Will AI replace policy analysts?


It's changing the junior work most. Microsoft ranks political scientists 9th of 785 occupations for AI applicability, and BLS projects that small field to shrink 2.0% from 2025 to 2035. Research summaries and memo drafts automate well. Judgment, stakeholder access and knowing the politics of a decision don't.


### How is AI used in the public sector?


Mostly in pilots and back-office work. Federal agencies reported 3,611 AI use cases in 2025, led by HHS and the VA, including record summaries and call-center bots. Code for America found nearly every state has piloted AI, but very few have built it into core operations yet.


### Is social work still a good major with AI?


Yes, if you're aiming for licensed or direct-practice roles. New York Fed data for 2024 shows recent social services graduates had 1.9% unemployment, among the lowest of any major, though early-career pay was about $43,000. Add data or program evaluation skills to widen your options.
